about: Parity vectors for app/static/js/engine/targets.js, generated from app/targets.py and app/target_rules.py by tests/data/gen_targets_vectors.py. Do not edit by hand: change the rules, then regenerate. Notes must match byte for byte; eer kcal is unrounded (compare within 1e-9 relative). A case's rules are catalogue keys: the API returns {id, ...tables.rules[key]} with id 'P-2' for the keys 'P-2d' and 'P-2n'.

S-2.opinion_note: age counted from the last day of the birth month

notes.W-1: Weight basis: {w:g} kg is in the healthy BMI range (BMI {bmi:.1f}) for {h:g} cm, so your actual weight is used for calories and protein.
notes.W-2: Weight basis: without a saved height your actual weight ({w:g} kg) is used. Add your height so the app can adjust for a weight above or below the healthy range.
notes.W-3: Weight basis: at BMI {bmi:.1f}, calories and protein use an adjusted weight of {ref:g} kg: the weight at BMI 25 for {h:g} cm ({w25:g} kg) plus a quarter of the weight above it. Guidelines leave the choice of weight to your care team (KDOQI 2020 1.1.6); this is the app's default.
notes.W-4: Weight basis: at BMI {bmi:.1f}, calories and protein use {ref:g} kg: your weight moved a quarter of the way toward the healthy range ({w185:g} kg at BMI 18.5), as in KDOQI's adjusted body weight. Gaining weight safely is a job for your renal dietitian.
notes.W-D: Enter your dry weight, measured after a dialysis session.
notes.N-1: Nutrition risk: {reasons}. The app moves protein and calories to the higher end. Ask your renal dietitian for a nutrition assessment and whether oral nutrition supplements would help (KDOQI 2020 4.1.1).
notes.N-1.low_bmi.older: BMI {bmi:.1f} is below {thr:g}, the low-weight cut-off from age 70 (GLIM 2019)
notes.N-1.weight_loss: you have lost {pct:.1f} % of your weight in 6 months
notes.N-1.frailty: frailty or low muscle mass is marked in your profile
notes.E-1: Calories: {kcal} kcal/day, the energy estimate for your age, sex, height, {ref:g} kg and activity ("{activity_label}") from the 2023 Dietary Reference Intakes ({kpk:.1f} kcal/kg), kept inside the kidney guideline range of 25–35 kcal/kg (KDOQI 2020 3.1.1).
notes.E-1.estimate: Energy estimate: {kcal} kcal/day for your age, sex, height, {ref:g} kg and activity ("{activity_label}") from the 2023 Dietary Reference Intakes ({kpk:.1f} kcal/kg), kept inside the kidney guideline range of 25–35 kcal/kg (KDOQI 2020 3.1.1). The calories suggested are in the next note.
notes.E-1.clamped: The estimate was {raw:.1f} kcal/kg, so it was set to {edge} kcal/kg.
notes.E-1.unspecified: Sex is not set, so the average of the female and male equations is used.
notes.E-2: Calories: 30 kcal/kg × {ref:g} kg = {kcal} kcal/day, the middle of the guideline range of 25–35 kcal/kg (KDOQI 2020 3.1.1). Add your birth month, sex, height and activity for a personal estimate.
notes.E-3: Calories: {kcal} kcal/day, raised to 30 kcal/kg × {ref:g} kg because of the nutrition risk above (ESPEN 2022; KDOQI 2020: 30–35 kcal/kg keeps protein balance).
notes.E-4: Peritoneal dialysis: {pdk} kcal/day absorbed from dialysis fluid was subtracted, so food calories are {kcal} of {total} kcal.
notes.E-4.floor: Peritoneal dialysis: about {pdk} kcal/day is absorbed from dialysis fluid, but food calories are kept at 20 kcal/kg × {ref:g} kg, so they are {kcal} of {total} kcal. Ask your renal dietitian about this.
notes.E-4.insulin: That glucose also needs insulin; your diabetes team plans for it.
notes.E-PD.missing: On peritoneal dialysis, add the calories your body absorbs from the dialysis fluid (ask your PD nurse) so the app can subtract them from food calories.
notes.P-1: Protein: {min}–{max} g/day (0.8–1.0 g/kg × {ref:g} kg). At stages 1–2 guidelines only ask you to avoid more than 1.3 g/kg (KDIGO 2024).
notes.P-2d: Protein: about {max} g/day (0.8 g/kg × {ref:g} kg) for CKD stages 3–5 with diabetes (KDIGO 2022 Rec 3.1.1; KDIGO 2024 Rec 3.3.1.1; ADA 2026 Rec 11.3). With diabetes, eating less than 0.8 g/kg is not recommended (ADA 2026): it risks muscle loss and low blood sugar. A lower amount (KDOQI 2020 3.0.2: 0.6–0.8) is only for people under close supervision by their care team. Avoid more than 1.3 g/kg (KDIGO 2024).
notes.P-2n: Protein: {min}–{max} g/day (0.6–0.8 g/kg × {ref:g} kg) for CKD stages 3–5. KDIGO 2024 Rec 3.3.1.1 suggests 0.8 g/kg. Going below 0.8 (KDOQI 2020 3.0.1: 0.55–0.6) needs close supervision by your care team, and is not for anyone who is unwell, in hospital recently or losing weight (KDIGO 2024 PP 3.3.1.3). Avoid more than 1.3 g/kg (KDIGO 2024).
notes.P-3: Protein: {min}–{max} g/day (1.0–1.2 g/kg × {ref:g} kg) on {mode_label} (KDOQI 2020 3.0.3/3.0.4). Dialysis removes protein, so more is needed, not less.
notes.P-5a: Protein raised to {lo}–{hi} g/kg ({min}–{max} g/day) because {why}: in older adults and people at risk of malnutrition, losing muscle is often the bigger danger (KDIGO 2024 PP 3.3.1.5; ADA 2026 Rec 13.11a: at least 0.8 g/kg). If your kidney function is falling fast, your team may still prefer a lower range.
notes.P-5a.both: you are 65 or older and at nutrition risk
notes.P-6: Protein raised to 1.2–1.3 g/kg ({min}–{max} g/day) because of the nutrition risk above (KDOQI 2000: 1.2 on hemodialysis, 1.2–1.3 on peritoneal dialysis).
notes.P-7: Protein: {min}–{max} g/day (0.8–1.0 g/kg × {ref:g} kg) for a working kidney transplant. No guideline sets a long-term number; low-protein diets are not used with anti-rejection medicines.
notes.P-7.graft: It is not raised further for age because your transplant's function is at stage {stage}; ask your team.
notes.K-0: Potassium: {k_mg} mg/day is a review ceiling for {stage_label}, not a prescription; no blood potassium from the last {days} days is saved. {potassium_note}
notes.K-0.labs_off: Potassium: {k_mg} mg/day is a review ceiling for {stage_label}, not a prescription; this server does not change it for blood test results. {potassium_note}
notes.K-1: Potassium: your blood potassium ({k:.1f} mmol/L on {date}) is low, so no potassium limit is set. Ask your care team whether to eat more potassium-rich foods or take a supplement (KDOQI 2020 6.4.2). {potassium_note}
notes.K-2: Potassium: your blood potassium ({k:.1f} mmol/L on {date}) is normal, so the review ceiling is relaxed one step to {k_mg} mg/day. While it stays normal there is no need to cut fruit and vegetables (KDOQI 2020 6.4.1; KDIGO 2024). {potassium_note}
notes.K-2.top: Potassium: your blood potassium ({k:.1f} mmol/L on {date}) is normal, so the review ceiling stays at {k_mg} mg/day, already the highest step for {stage_label}. While it stays normal there is no need to cut fruit and vegetables (KDOQI 2020 6.4.1; KDIGO 2024). {potassium_note}
notes.K-2h: Potassium: your blood potassium ({k:.1f} mmol/L on {date}) is normal, but you have had high potassium before or take a potassium binder, so the ceiling stays at {k_mg} mg/day; processed foods with potassium additives matter most (KDIGO 2024 PP 3.11.5.2). {potassium_note}
notes.K-3: Potassium: your blood potassium ({k:.1f} mmol/L on {date}) is above normal (over 5.0), so the ceiling is {k_mg} mg/day. Check processed foods with potassium additives, salt substitutes and large portions first; your team may also review medicines (KDIGO 2024 Figure 32). {potassium_note}
notes.K-4: Potassium: your blood potassium ({k:.1f} mmol/L on {date}) is high (over 5.5), so the ceiling is {k_mg} mg/day. Tell your care team; they may change medicines or start a potassium binder. {potassium_note}
notes.K-5: Potassium: {k:.1f} mmol/L on {date} is dangerously high. {urgency} The ceiling is set to {k_mg} mg/day until your team gives you a number. {potassium_note}
notes.K-5.urgent: Contact your care team today: this result should be repeated within 24 hours, and if you feel unwell (weakness, palpitations or an irregular pulse) get urgent medical care now (KDIGO 2024 Table 28).
notes.K-5.emergency: Get urgent medical care now, especially with weakness, palpitations or an irregular pulse (KDIGO 2024 Table 28).
notes.K-5.alert: Potassium {k:.1f} mmol/L on {date} is dangerously high. {urgency}
notes.PH-0: Phosphorus: {p_mg} mg/day (guideline range 800–1000 mg when phosphate runs high); no phosphate result from the last {days} days is saved. Avoiding phosphate additives matters more than the total because additive phosphorus is almost fully absorbed.
notes.PH-0.labs_off: Phosphorus: {p_mg} mg/day (guideline range 800–1000 mg when phosphate runs high); this server does not change it for blood test results. Avoiding phosphate additives matters more than the total because additive phosphorus is almost fully absorbed.
notes.PH-T: Phosphorus: not limited after a kidney transplant unless your phosphate is high; low phosphate is common in the first months (KDOQI 2020 6.3.3).
notes.PH-1: Phosphorus: your phosphate ({p:.1f} mg/dL on {date}) is low, so no phosphorus limit is set. Ask your team whether to eat more phosphorus or take a supplement (KDOQI 2020 6.3.3).
notes.PH-2: Phosphorus: your phosphate ({p:.1f} mg/dL on {date}) is normal; {p_mg_or_none} is a review ceiling. Keep avoiding phosphate additives (KDOQI 2020 6.3.1–6.3.2).
notes.PH-2.none: Phosphorus: your phosphate ({p:.1f} mg/dL on {date}) is normal, so no phosphorus limit is set after a kidney transplant. Keep avoiding phosphate additives (KDOQI 2020 6.3.1–6.3.2).
notes.PH-3: Phosphorus: your phosphate ({p:.1f} mg/dL on {date}) is above normal (over 4.5), so the target is 800 mg/day, the low end of the 800–1000 mg range (KDOQI 2003; KDIGO 2017). Cut phosphate additives first and take binders with meals as prescribed. On dialysis keep protein up by choosing foods with little phosphorus per gram of protein (egg whites, fresh meat and fish).
notes.NA-1: Sodium: 2000 mg/day for every adult with CKD, whatever the age or sex (KDIGO 2024; KDOQI 2020 6.5.1: under 2300 mg).
notes.CA-0: Calcium: 1000 mg/day. Add your birth month and sex for the amount recommended for your age.
notes.CA-1: Calcium: at most 1000 mg/day in total, counting calcium-based binders and supplements (KDOQI 2020 6.2.1: 800–1000 mg at stages 3–4 when not taking active vitamin D such as calcitriol). At these stages it does not change with age or sex.
notes.CA-2: Calcium: 1000 mg/day in total as a starting point; at stage 5 and on dialysis your team adjusts it to avoid high calcium, counting binders and vitamin D medicines (KDOQI 2020 6.2.2 covers dialysis; for stage 5 without dialysis this is the app's default).
notes.CA-3: Calcium: {rda}–{ul} mg/day: the general recommendation for your age and sex ({rda} mg) up to the safe upper limit ({ul} mg) (Dietary Reference Intakes 2011).
notes.F-0: Fluid: no limit without dialysis unless your care team sets one.
notes.F-0o: Fluid: no limit without dialysis unless your care team sets one. Thirst fades with age: unless your team limits fluid, or you have heart failure or swelling, aim for at least {floor} of drinks a day (ESPEN 2022).
notes.F-1: Fluid: 1000 mL plus your 24-hour urine volume; 1500 mL assumes about 500 mL of urine. Enter your urine volume or ask your dialysis unit for your allowance.
notes.F-2: Fluid: 1000 mL + your {u} mL of urine = {fluid} mL/day, the usual hemodialysis allowance; your unit may set a different number.
notes.F-3: Fluid: about 2000 mL/day on peritoneal dialysis. Enter your daily urine volume and ultrafiltration for a personal number.
notes.F-4: Fluid: urine {u} mL + ultrafiltration {uf} mL = {fluid} mL/day, about what your body removes each day. Check it with your PD nurse.
notes.C-1.diabetes: Carbohydrate: 45 % of calories ÷ 4 kcal/g = {carbs} g/day, about {per_meal} g per meal for carb counting; your insulin-to-carb ratio decides the real per-meal number.
notes.FB-1: Fiber: at least {fib} g/day (14 g per 1000 kcal, ADA 2026). When potassium is limited, get it from low-potassium fruit, vegetables and grains.
notes.L-ALB: Low albumin can also come from inflammation or protein lost in urine, not only from diet (KDOQI 2020 1.2.1). Labs measure albumin in different ways; ask your team whether this result counts as low for your lab.
notes.L-BIC22: Bicarbonate {b:.1f} mmol/L is below 22: acid builds up as kidneys fail. {fv}Your team may prescribe bicarbonate (KDOQI 2020 6.1.2).
notes.L-BIC22.fv: More fruit and vegetables lower the acid load (KDOQI 2020 6.1.1){k_caveat}.
notes.L-BIC22.k_caveat: (your potassium is high, so ask your team first)
notes.L-BIC18: Bicarbonate {b:.1f} mmol/L is below 18. KDIGO 2024 says treatment should be considered at this level (practice point 3.10.1); tell your care team.
notes.L-UACR: Urine albumin {uacr:.1f} {unit} (as entered) is category {cat} ({cat_label}). It does not change food targets but is a reason to keep sodium low (KDOQI 2020 6.5.2).
notes.L-UACR.a3_low_albumin: With low blood albumin this can mean protein is lost in urine; your team may set protein differently.
notes.L-A1C: A1c and CGM readings do not change these food targets; in advanced CKD A1c is less reliable (KDIGO 2022 PP 2.1.2).
notes.END: These are starting points only — confirm every target with your nephrologist and renal dietitian.

tables.potassium_note: Only restrict potassium if your blood potassium is high; your care team sets the number.

out_of_scope_pregnancy.message: Targets are not suggested during pregnancy or breastfeeding: needs for energy, protein, calcium and fluid change, and kidney disease in pregnancy needs specialist care. Ask your kidney and maternity teams for targets; you can still enter them by hand.

out_of_scope_under_18.message: Targets are not suggested for people under 18: children need more protein and energy to grow, and kidney guidelines for children are different. Ask your child's kidney team; you can still enter targets by hand.

out_of_scope_early_transplant.message: Your kidney transplant was less than 12 weeks ago. In the first weeks your transplant team sets a recovery diet, usually higher in protein, so the app does not suggest targets yet. You can still enter targets by hand.

Phosphorus: your phosphate (6.0 mg/dL on Oct 5, 2026) is above normal (over 4.5), so the target is 800 mg/day, the low end of the 800–1000 mg range (KDOQI 2003; KDIGO 2017). Carbohydrate: 45 % of calories ÷ 4 kcal/g = 236 g/day, about 60 g per meal for carb counting; your insulin-to-carb ratio decides the real per-meal number.
Fiber: at least 29 g/day (14 g per 1000 kcal, ADA 2026). When potassium is limited, get it from low-potassium fruit, vegetables and grains.

Low albumin can also come from inflammation or protein lost in urine, not only from diet (KDOQI 2020 1.2.1). Labs measure albumin in different ways; ask your team whether this result counts as low for your lab.

Bicarbonate 16.0 mmol/L is below 22: acid builds up as kidneys fail. More fruit and vegetables lower the acid load (KDOQI 2020 6.1.1) (your potassium is high, so ask your team first). Your team may prescribe bicarbonate (KDOQI 2020 6.1.2).
Bicarbonate 16.0 mmol/L is below 18. KDIGO 2024 says treatment should be considered at this level (practice point 3.10.1); tell your care team.

Urine albumin 500.0 mg/g (as entered) is category A3 (severely increased). It does not change food targets but is a reason to keep sodium low (KDOQI 2020 6.5.2). With low blood albumin this can mean protein is lost in urine; your team may set protein differently.
A1c and CGM readings do not change these food targets; in advanced CKD A1c is less reliable (KDIGO 2022 PP 2.1.2).

Calories: 1460 kcal/day, the energy estimate for your age, sex, height, 41.6 kg and activity ("inactive") from the 2023 Dietary Reference Intakes (35.0 kcal/kg), kept inside the kidney guideline range of 25–35 kcal/kg (KDOQI 2020 3.1.1). The estimate was 40.0 kcal/kg, so it was set to 35 kcal/kg. Sex is not set, so the average of the female and male equations is used.

Protein: about 33 g/day (0.8 g/kg × 41.6 kg) for CKD stages 3–5 with diabetes (KDIGO 2022 Rec 3.1.1; KDIGO 2024 Rec 3.3.1.1; ADA 2026 Rec 11.3). With diabetes, eating less than 0.8 g/kg is not recommended (ADA 2026): it risks muscle loss and low blood sugar. A lower amount (KDOQI 2020 3.0.2: 0.6–0.8) is only for people under close supervision by their care team. Avoid more than 1.3 g/kg (KDIGO 2024).

Protein raised to 0.8–1.0 g/kg (33–42 g/day) because of the nutrition risk above: in older adults and people at risk of malnutrition, losing muscle is often the bigger danger (KDIGO 2024 PP 3.3.1.5; ADA 2026 Rec 13.11a: at least 0.8 g/kg). If your kidney function is falling fast, your team may still prefer a lower range.

Potassium: 4000 mg/day is a review ceiling for stage 3a, not a prescription; no blood potassium from the last 90 days is saved. Only restrict potassium if your blood potassium is high; your care team sets the number.

Phosphorus: 1000 mg/day (guideline range 800–1000 mg when phosphate runs high); no phosphate result from the last 90 days is saved. Avoiding phosphate additives matters more than the total because additive phosphorus is almost fully absorbed.
Sodium: 2000 mg/day for every adult with CKD, whatever the age or sex (KDIGO 2024; KDOQI 2020 6.5.1: under 2300 mg).

Calcium: at most 1000 mg/day in total, counting calcium-based binders and supplements (KDOQI 2020 6.2.1: 800–1000 mg at stages 3–4 when not taking active vitamin D such as calcitriol). At these stages it does not change with age or sex.
Fluid: no limit without dialysis unless your care team sets one.
Carbohydrate: 45 % of calories ÷ 4 kcal/g = 164 g/day, about 40 g per meal for carb counting; your insulin-to-carb ratio decides the real per-meal number.
Fiber: at least 20 g/day (14 g per 1000 kcal, ADA 2026). When potassium is limited, get it from low-potassium fruit, vegetables and grains.
Urine albumin 705.6 mg/g (as entered) is category A3 (severely increased). It does not change food targets but is a reason to keep sodium low (KDOQI 2020 6.5.2).
A1c and CGM readings do not change these food targets; in advanced CKD A1c is less reliable (KDIGO 2022 PP 2.1.2).
